title: If you cut your grass with a lawn mower, did you really cut the grass?
author: zanemoore575
selftext:
So here I am mowing me lawns on a beauty of a day here In NZ! Just trimming up the edges before I bring the mower round. 

And then it came to me. 

I’m cutting my grass with a line trimmer.  
And interestingly, my neighbour, an elderly gentleman, does all the edges of his lawn with a knife. Seriously, he doesn’t own a line trimmer. 

Now, are are my lawns edges better than his? Not really. His edges actually look tidier. The difference is, I can finish my lawns in about 20 minutes. 

That doesn’t mean his method or mine is wrong, it’s just different methods. My neighbour enjoys using a knife to trim the grass around the edges. And I wouldn’t even know where to start doing it that way. 

I use the machine to get the result. 

So, if your using AI tools to build a game your genuinely passionate about, don’t worry about the hate from the anti-ai crowd. 

There are literally vegetarians out here copping hate for trying to bring less harm and brutality to animals 😅🗿

So if people can hate on that, they’ll find a reason to criticise you too xD 

Ignore em, build something truly great.  
Cheers dudes 🤙🤙

A lot don’t let you change this anymore because it can cause looping and other problems. https://benchlm.ai/blog/posts/llm-temperature

comments.author: BobFuel
comments.body:
Look, I'm not anti-ai, but this comparison just doesn't work.

A lawn mower is a tool that you still need to operate during the whole process. Ai is more like one of those automatic Roomba-landmowers, or even an entire other person hired to do it for you. 

Sure you can ask it/them to do things a certain way, but at the end of the day you're not actively participating during the process of "cutting the grass" itself, so it's not really comparable 

And I'd argue some people probably do prefer cutting grass themselves, I don't know I'm not really interested in landscaping, but I'm sure some people are, and that's ok too

All in all, jabs and bad comparisons like this (from both pro and anti AI) only makes each side sound more dumb to the other

replies.author: NotARedditor6969
replies.body:
\> A lawn mower is a tool that you still need to operate during the whole process. Ai is more like one of those automatic Roomba-landmowers, or even an entire other person hired to do it for you.

Have you actually tried to make anything remotely complex with AI? Because this reads like someone who hasn't.

You can't just prompt "Make me Resident Evil 9" and expect something of even remotely comparable quality or depth.

You're still actively participating throughout the development process. You're designing, directing, testing, iterating, identifying problems, evaluating solutions and making creative decisions.

The fact that you're delegating aspects of the execution doesn't mean you've removed yourself from the creative process.

By that logic, a film director isn't actively participating in making a film because someone else is operating the camera.

replies.body:
Your original argument is that you still need to operate the lawnmower, but you don’t operate the AI, or don’t operate it enough so it’s better compared to a Roomba. Because you made this criticism, I have a suspicion that you’re using your AI like a Roomba. It’s a personal skill issue rather than an accurate criticism.

When you use a lawnmower, you don’t wave the blades in a tubular fashion - the mower does it for you. You don’t exactly know how the mower cuts grass beneath the machine, kind of like how AI writes code. But you still need to know how to operate the mower, which is similar to knowing how to operate the CLI. You’ll still need to control how much mowing you’d do is considered done, which is similar to writing specs to feed the AI and verify if the work done complies with your specs.

So, I think the comparison, while snarky, is apt. I’m sorry for the personal jab, but I think the way you talk about AI is a tell that you’re handing agency away rather than it taking the agency from you.

replies.author: BobFuel
replies.body:
Again, you're assuming things. 

>or don’t operate it enough

I'm not talking about "enough" vs "not enough". I'm not sharing a jugement or subjective value on AI usage, not saying it is good or bad, and I am not suggesting AI is taking agency from me personally. It's simply that there's a difference between "monitoring" an AI and "operating" a deterministic tool. It's apples and oranges.

AI works more like monitoring a newly hired junior: you still need to understand your scope, the project, the tasks. You still need to guide the junior through the tasks it's taking over from you and still need to control the output.

But it's not like operating a tool. You don't "monitor" a regular landmower. Or a pen, or a knife, or even heavy machinery. You're not checking it's output after the fact, because you are still active in the entire process of creating said output **using** it. You also can't ask for it's feedback, review or suggestions on any of the things you're doing, because the thing can't talk back.

I stick to what I said, AI is closer to monitoring a Roomba than it is to operating a landmower. A Roomba may not be the best comparison either, but it's still a better one

comments.author: StateQuiet7463
comments.body:
This is a false equivalence fallacy.   
  
Your example involves two people doing the work still, just using different levels of tools to get the job done.   
  
A general tool has no way of making decisions and typically needs an operator; the line trimmer needs you to hold and operate it to perform work. 

AI can do things like generate all the code for you; it replaces the need to exert effort in for tasks it is used on, you can do literally anything else while it works like take a nap.   
  
The more accurate situation is you doing the work with the line trimmer vs a neighbor who has a robot that cuts their grass for them. Your neighbor is then free to do something else like tend to the garden. His garden ends up looking amazing since they no longer had to worry about the lawn's upkeep. 

That is where the real benefit lies, you can have the AI handle things while you look over other areas of the game. 

But this is also why people tend to not like when AI is used.   
  
Yes, AI can be used to deliver software in a timely manner or make more elaborate features people want.   
  
Yes, AI can help smaller devs get more work done without burning themselves out. 

Yes, AI in some respects can outperform a person in a lot of ways. 

But people without knowledge use it to work on something, claim they made it as if they had done all the work themselves. This is where people get upset. Which is understandable.   
  
Before AI, people had to learn how to do everything themselves or find people who knew how to do something and work with them. It was a lot more effort intensive, which is a limitation that had to be worked around. People also don't want to disclose AI.   
  
So, it feels like people are taking a shortcut without putting in the hard work. This devalues the work in the eyes of some people since how things are made does factor into how things are valued. If you made your game entirely by hand, it would take longer, it may not be as feature rich, but people would value it due to the effort involved. Other people value the end result more and thus tend to be being more accepting of AI use. 

The other concern is if someone who has no idea how to do something like coding and relies entirely on the AI to do all of it; they are then unable to fix any issues manually when AI is unable to fix them. Which is something I run into often when working on more elaborate projects. Some things I find it easier to fix myself since I know exactly what I want while the AI simply makes educated guesses at my intent.   
  
With AI You can end up in a technical debt hole you cannot dig yourself out of when the AI starts becoming a hurdle instead of aiding you. 

At the end of the day, you need to ask yourself what you value more.   
  
Making something entirely yourself even if it means taking much longer to complete or getting it done as quickly as possible? 

Making it yourself has its own risks, we have seen vaporware or abandonware or projects that failed to match expectations. But it has a lot of reward, you did everything yourself and that takes a lot of effort. 

Having AI help you make something, it removes some of the value in some respects. However, there is value in ensuring the software is delivered, all features are implemented and the end result was realized.   
  
Both require a fair amount of effort, one simply reduces the effort required at the expense of you being able to claim you made it entirely yourself or applied all of your technical knowledge that you had leaned.
